warmup.q: fun requireCurrency(c: String?) { if (c == null) throw IllegalArgumentException() }. After requireCurrency(currency), you write currency.uppercase() where currency is a String?. What happens?
options: It compiles: the compiler sees the throw inside requireCurrency
Compile error: currency is still a String? to the compiler
It compiles, and throws NullPointerException if currency is null
warmup.why: The compiler analyzes each function on its own. It doesn't look inside requireCurrency to learn that a normal return means c != null, so currency stays nullable and you get only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'. The standard library's require gets the smart cast because it declares a contract, which is the first half of this lesson.

sections.h: Your own check functions teach the compiler nothing
sections.html:
The standard library's require(currency != null) makes currency usable as a String on the next line. Write the same check in your own function, and the compiler forgets it:

Java
// Java's type system doesn't track null at all, so the question never comes up
static void requireCurrency(String currency) {
    if (currency == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency missing");
}

requireCurrency(currency);
System.out.println(currency.toUpperCase());      // compiles, as everything does
Kotlin
fun requireCurrencyPlain(currency: String?) {
    if (currency == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("currency missing")
}

requireCurrencyPlain(currency)
println(currency.uppercase())
// error: only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'.

The feature that fails here is the smart cast: after a check such as if (x != null), the compiler treats x as the narrower type. It does that only for checks it can see in the current function. It never reads the body of a function you call, because that body may change, or live in another module.

A contract closes the gap. It is a contract { } block, written as the first statement of a function, that states something about the function's behavior that callers may rely on. Two kinds matter in practice. returns() implies (currency != null) says: if this function returns normally, the condition holds. callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) says: the lambda runs exactly once, during this call, and is not stored. The other kinds are AT_MOST_ONCE, AT_LEAST_ONCE and UNKNOWN.

Java
// Java can't assign a local inside a lambda at all:
// "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final"
String[] label = new String[1];
ContractsDemoKt.once(() -> { label[0] = "batch-17"; return Unit.INSTANCE; });
Kotlin
@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun requireCurrency(currency: String?) {
    contract { returns() implies (currency != null) }
    if (currency == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("currency missing")
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
inline fun <T> once(block: () -> T): T {
    contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) }
    return block()
}

val label: String
once { label = "batch-17" }     // allowed: the block runs exactly once

This is how require, check, requireNotNull, run, let and apply work in the standard library. Contracts are still Experimental in Kotlin 2.4: the 2.4.0 notes say so, and without @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) every part of the block fails with this declaration needs opt-in. No compiler flag is needed, only the annotation.

steps: Run ContractsDemo (or ContractsDemoJava, which calls the same Kotlin functions).
Wrong move 1: call requireCurrencyPlain(currency) instead of requireCurrency(currency). Predict the error, run, undo.
Wrong move 2: delete the contract { callsInPlace(...) } line in once. once is still inline. Predict whether that is enough, run, undo.
Wrong move 3: delete the @OptIn above isCaptured, run, undo.

code.title: ContractsDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind import kotlin.contracts.contract sealed interface PaymentEvent data class Captured(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PaymentEvent data class Failed(val paymentId: String, val reason: String) : PaymentEvent fun lookupCurrency(merchant: String): String? = if (merchant.startsWith("m-")) "eur" else null /** Checks, but tells the compiler nothing. */ fun requireCurrencyPlain(currency: String?) { if (currency == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("currency missing") } /** The same check, plus a promise: if this returns, currency was not null. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun requireCurrency(currency: String?) { contract { returns() implies (currency != null) } if (currency == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("currency missing") } /** A promise about the receiver: a true result means this is a Captured. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun PaymentEvent.isCaptured(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@isCaptured is Captured) } return this is Captured } /** A promise about the lambda: it runs exactly once, during this call. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> once(block: () -> T): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } return block() } fun main() { val currency = lookupCurrency("m-981") requireCurrency(currency) println("currency = ${currency.uppercase()}") // smart cast to String val event: PaymentEvent = Captured("pay_7", 1_999) if (event.isCaptured()) println("captured ${event.amountMinor}") // smart cast to Captured val label: String // a val, assigned inside a lambda once { label = "batch-17" } println("label = $label") // Wrong moves, one at a time. Predict the error, run, undo. // 1. Call requireCurrencyPlain(currency) instead of requireCurrency(currency). // 2. Delete the line `contract { callsInPlace(...) }` in once. // 3. Delete @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) above isCaptured. }

alt.title: ContractsDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; import kotlin.Unit; /** * Java twin of ContractsDemo.kt. Java has no contracts. It has no null checks in the type system to * satisfy, its instanceof pattern binds a new variable instead of smart-casting, and a lambda may * not assign a local variable at all. */ public class ContractsDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { String currency = ContractsDemoKt.lookupCurrency("m-981"); ContractsDemoKt.requireCurrency(currency); // to Java: a void method, nothing more System.out.println("currency = " + currency.toUpperCase()); PaymentEvent event = new Captured("pay_7", 1_999); if (event instanceof Captured c) { // the pattern binds c: no promise needed System.out.println("captured " + c.getAmountMinor()); } // String label; once(() -> { label = "x"; ... }) would not compile: // "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final" String[] label = new String[1]; ContractsDemoKt.once(() -> { label[0] = "batch-17"; return Unit.INSTANCE; }); System.out.println("label = " + label[0]); } }

try.expect: The demo prints currency = EUR, captured 1999 and label = batch-17. Move 1 fails on currency.uppercase() with the nullable-receiver error. Move 2 fails with 'val' cannot be reassigned. and variable 'label' must be initialized.: being inline doesn't tell the compiler how many times the body calls block. Move 3 fails with this declaration needs opt-in. Its usage must be marked with '@kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts' or '@OptIn(kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts::class)'.

sections.h: The compiler trusts a contract and never checks it
sections.html:
A contract is a promise, and the compiler doesn't check the body against it. The design document, KEEP-139, says the compiler "trusts contracts unconditionally" and that the programmer is "responsible for writing correct and sound contracts". Formal verification is listed as a non-goal. So this compiles without a single warning:

Java
// Java's version of the same lie: a check that always says yes, and a cast that believes it
static boolean lyingIsCaptured(PaymentEvent e) { return true; }

if (lyingIsCaptured(failed)) {
    Captured c = (Captured) failed;              // ClassCastException
}
Kotlin
@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun PaymentEvent.lyingIsCaptured(): Boolean {
    contract { returns(true) implies (this@lyingIsCaptured is Captured) }
    return true                                  // the lie
}

if (failed.lyingIsCaptured()) println(failed.amountMinor)   // ClassCastException

The smart cast to Captured lets failed.amountMinor compile. At run time the JVM still checks the cast it was given, and Failed is not a Captured: class ...Failed cannot be cast to class ...Captured. A contract can't make a wrong value right. It moves the cast from your code, where a reviewer sees it, into a promise inside another function.

Look one level down and the reason is plain. javap -c on the honest isCaptured shows a null check on the receiver, then instanceof Captured and ireturn: no trace of the contract. The contract lives in the Kotlin metadata of the class file, which only the Kotlin compiler reads when it compiles a caller. Java callers never see it, and nothing at run time enforces it.

The K2 compiler does catch some callsInPlace mistakes, as warnings. A block declared EXACTLY_ONCE but called twice gets wrong invocation kind 'EXACTLY_ONCE' for 'block: () -> Unit' specified, the actual invocation kind is 'AT_LEAST_ONCE'. A block declared in place but stored in a list gets leaked in-place lambda 'block: () -> Unit'. Nothing checks returns ... implies. And the block must come first: anything before it is contract should be the first statement.

So write contracts the way the standard library does: tiny functions whose body is the condition itself, such as if (!condition) throw ..., so a reader can check the promise in one glance. Kotlin 2.2.20 added more Experimental forms (contracts on property accessors, returnsNotNull(), holdsIn). The last two need a second opt-in, ExperimentalExtendedContracts.

try.title: Make a contract lie
steps: Run LyingContractDemo. Before you do, predict: compile error, a warning, or a run-time failure?
Run LyingContractDemoJava, which tells the same lie in Java with a cast, then calls the Kotlin function.
Run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContractsDemoKt from labs/ and read isCaptured. Where is the contract?

code.title: LyingContractDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.contract /** A contract that lies. The compiler checks neither the promise nor the body. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun PaymentEvent.lyingIsCaptured(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@lyingIsCaptured is Captured) } return true } fun main() { val failed: PaymentEvent = Failed("pay_8", "insufficient funds") try { if (failed.lyingIsCaptured()) println("captured ${failed.amountMinor}") } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: LyingContractDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; /** * Java twin of LyingContractDemo.kt. Java's version of the same lie is a helper that answers true * and a cast that trusts it. In both languages the cast is the line that fails at run time. */ public class LyingContractDemoJava { static boolean lyingIsCaptured(PaymentEvent e) { return true; } public static void main(String[] args) { PaymentEvent failed = new Failed("pay_8", "insufficient funds"); try { if (lyingIsCaptured(failed)) { Captured c = (Captured) failed; // Java makes you write the cast yourself System.out.println("captured " + c.getAmountMinor()); } } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); } // the Kotlin function, seen from Java: just a boolean method, the contract is gone System.out.println("Kotlin lyingIsCaptured from Java: " + LyingContractDemoKt.lyingIsCaptured(failed)); } }

try.expect: It compiles cleanly and fails at run time with ClassCastException: class workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.Failed cannot be cast to class workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.Captured. The Java twin fails the same way, then prints Kotlin lyingIsCaptured from Java: true: to Java it's a boolean method. In javap, isCaptured is a null check on the receiver, then instanceof and ireturn. The contract isn't in the bytecode at all.

sections.h: Context parameters: arguments the compiler passes for you
sections.html:
Some values have to reach almost every function in a request: a logger, the transaction id, a clock. Passed by hand, they turn every signature into plumbing:

Java
boolean authorize(Logger logger, TxId tx, Payment payment, String merchant) { ... }

String checkout(Logger logger, TxId tx, Payment payment, String merchant) {
    boolean ok = authorize(logger, tx, payment, merchant);   // pass both on, by hand
    audit(logger, "checkout " + tx.value());
    return ok ? "APPROVED" : "DECLINED";
}
Kotlin
context(logger: Logger, tx: TxId)
fun Payment.authorize(merchant: String): Boolean {
    logger.log("[${tx.value}] authorizing $amountMinor for $merchant")
    return amountMinor < 100_000
}

context(logger: Logger, tx: TxId)
fun checkout(payment: Payment, merchant: String): String {
    val approved = payment.authorize(merchant)               // logger and tx flow on by themselves
    audit("checkout ${tx.value}")
    return if (approved) "APPROVED" else "DECLINED"
}

A context parameter is a parameter the caller doesn't write. You declare it in context(...) before fun, with a name and a type. At each call, the compiler finds a value of that type in the caller's surroundings and passes it: an enclosing function's own context parameter (as in checkout above), a context(console, TxId("tx-42")) { ... } block from the standard library, or an implicit receiver, such as the this of a with(console) { ... } block. The value it finds is called the context argument. Inside the function, you use the parameter by its name. If you don't need a name, write _ and read the value with contextOf<Logger>().

The docs describe them as dependencies that are "implicitly available in the surrounding context". On the JVM there is nothing implicit about them, as the figure shows. They become ordinary leading parameters: the context parameters first, then the extension receiver, then the value parameters. javap prints authorize(Logger, TxId, Payment, String), and Java calls it by passing all four.

The status changed a lot in a short time. Context parameters were a preview in Kotlin 2.2.0 behind -Xcontext-parameters, and became Stable in 2.4.0, "except for context arguments and callable references". So in 2.4 you need no flag. The old flag now earns warning: the argument '-Xcontext-parameters' is redundant for the current language version 2.4., which tells you an older build file is still around.

sections.h: Resolution rules, limits, and when to use them
sections.html:
The compiler resolves context arguments by type, so two values of the same type in the same scope are a problem. context(a, b) { use() } with two Loggers fails with multiple potential context arguments for 'l: Logger' in scope. The docs give the rule: if several compatible values exist at the same scope level, the compiler reports an ambiguity. A nearer scope still wins over an outer one: in context(a) { context(b) { note("x") } } the inner b is used. That's a reason to give context parameters specific types: a TxId class instead of a bare String, an AuditLog interface instead of (String) -> Unit.

A few things are not allowed. Constructors can't have context parameters (context parameters on primary constructors are unsupported.). A property can have them only without a backing field, so it has to be a computed getter (property with context parameters cannot be initialized because it has no backing field.). And two parts are still not stable in 2.4: passing a context argument explicitly by name, behind -Xexplicit-context-arguments, and callable references such as ::checkout. Leave both alone in production code for now.

One change in 2.3.20 can surprise you if you migrate older code. Overload resolution used to treat a declaration with context parameters as more specific than one without. The 2.3.20 notes say that rule no longer applies, so a pair of overloads that differed only by a context may become ambiguous.

The JVM shape has two consequences. Java code can call these functions, as long as it passes every argument. And adding a context parameter to a public function changes its JVM signature, exactly like adding a parameter, so already-compiled callers break. Treat it as an API change.

Where do they fit in a Quarkus service? Not for business dependencies: a PaymentRepository belongs in the constructor, where CDI injects it once. Context parameters suit values that belong to the current unit of work and are needed by many small functions: the transaction or trace id, an audit sink, a Clock for tests, the TxContext the lab uses. They are cheap, they are visible in every signature, and the compiler checks them, which a ThreadLocal or a static MDC never does.

A check to finish: fun handle(req: AuthRequest) = with(AuditLog { println(it) }) { context(TxContext("tx-9")) { req.authorize(10_000) } }. Will it compile, and where does each context argument come from? (Answer: it compiles. The AuditLog comes from the implicit receiver of with, and the TxContext from the context(...) block. Each type has exactly one candidate.)

analogy: A contract is a signed statement from a colleague: "if my check returns, the field is filled in". The compiler files it and never opens the folder to see whether it's true, so a false statement passes every gate until the moment someone relies on it. A context parameter is the badge you wear inside a building: doors (functions) check that you have one of the right kind and let you through without asking for it again. The analogy breaks at the JVM: there the badge is just one more argument handed to every function, and Java has to hand it over in person.
world: Payment validation code is full of checks that should narrow types: ensure(req.currency != null, "CURRENCY_MISSING") followed by code that uses the currency. A small contract-backed ensure gives you that without a !! on every line, and with a stable error code for the API response. Context parameters fit the values your Quarkus request handlers drag through every layer today: the transaction id, the merchant id for logs, an audit sink, a Clock your tests can freeze. A Temporal activity implementation could open one context(audit, TxContext(paymentId)) { ... } block and call ten helpers that never mention either. Keep injected services in constructors, where CDI puts them, and keep contracts tiny, because nobody checks them but you.
mistake:
Writing a contract that is almost true. A team adds returns(true) implies (this@isFinal is Settled) to isFinal(), which returns true for Settled and, after a later change, also for Cancelled. Every caller that wrote if (p.isFinal()) p.settledAt still compiles. It fails only at run time, with a ClassCastException, on the first cancelled payment:

Java
// Java makes the risky cast visible at every call site, where review can see it
if (p.isFinal()) { Instant at = ((Settled) p).getSettledAt(); }
Kotlin
if (p.isFinal()) println(p.settledAt)   // the cast is hidden in isFinal's contract

The compiler trusts contracts unconditionally, so a change to the body never revisits the promise. Keep the body of a contract function identical to its promise (return this is Settled), and add a unit test that feeds each subtype through it.

compare.title: A validation helper with an audit trail: Java parameters vs Kotlin contracts and context parameters

java.title: Authorize.java
java.html: final class Authorize { static void ensure(boolean condition, String code, Supplier<String> message) { if (!condition) throw new PaymentRejected(code, message.get()); } static Decision authorize(AuditLog audit, TxContext tx, AuthRequest req, long limitMinor) { try { ensure(req.amountMinor() <= limitMinor, "OVER_LIMIT", () -> "over the limit"); ensure(req.currency() != null, "CURRENCY_MISSING", () -> "currency is required"); audit.record("[" + tx.txId() + "] approved " + req.currency().toUpperCase()); return Decision.APPROVED; } catch (PaymentRejected e) { audit.record("[" + tx.txId() + "] rejected " + e.code()); return Decision.rejected(e.code()); } } }

kotlin.title: Authorize.kt
kotlin.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun ensure(condition: Boolean, code: String, lazyMessage: () -> String) { contract { returns() implies condition callsInPlace(lazyMessage, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) } if (!condition) throw PaymentRejected(code, lazyMessage()) } context(audit: AuditLog, tx: TxContext) fun AuthRequest.authorize(limitMinor: Long): Decision = try { ensure(amountMinor <= limitMinor, "OVER_LIMIT") { "over the limit" } ensure(currency != null, "CURRENCY_MISSING") { "currency is required" } audit.record("[${tx.txId}] approved ${currency.uppercase()}") // smart cast Decision.Approved } catch (e: PaymentRejected) { audit.record("[${tx.txId}] rejected ${e.code}") Decision.Rejected(e.code) }

compare.note: The Java version compiles because Java doesn't track null, so req.currency().toUpperCase() is accepted whether or not the check ran. The Kotlin version compiles only because the contract tells the compiler that ensure returns only when its condition holds. Kotlin's ensure is inline, so the message lambda costs nothing on the happy path; Java builds a Supplier on every call. The audit log and transaction appear in Java's signature as two extra parameters that every caller passes on. In Kotlin they are context parameters, filled in by the compiler, and they still compile to exactly those two leading parameters, so Java can call the Kotlin authorize with authorize(audit, tx, req, limitMinor).

worked.title: Replace a ThreadLocal transaction id with a context parameter

steps.say: A service keeps the current transaction id in a ThreadLocal, so deep helpers can log it. It works until a helper runs on another thread, or a test forgets to set it, and then the log says tx=null. The compiler can't help, because nothing in the signature says the value is needed.
steps.code: final class Tx { static final ThreadLocal<String> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>(); } static void note(String line) { System.out.println("[" + Tx.CURRENT.get() + "] " + line); // null if nobody set it }

alt.html: object Tx { val current = ThreadLocal<String>() } fun note(line: String) { println("[${Tx.current.get()}] $line") // null if nobody set it }

steps.say: Make the need part of the signature. The helper declares a context parameter, and so does every function that calls it, until you reach the place that knows the transaction.
steps.code: class TxContext(val txId: String) // 1. the helper declares what it needs context(tx: TxContext) fun note(line: String) = println("[${tx.txId}] $line") // 2. callers in between declare it too, and never pass it by hand context(tx: TxContext) fun capture(paymentId: String) { note("capturing $paymentId") }

alt.html: // Java's honest equivalent: an explicit parameter on every function in the chain record TxContext(String txId) {} static void note(TxContext tx, String line) { System.out.println("[" + tx.txId() + "] " + line); } static void capture(TxContext tx, String paymentId) { note(tx, "capturing " + paymentId); }

steps.say: Open the context once, where the transaction starts: the Kafka listener or the REST resource. Forgetting it is now a compile error, no context argument for 'tx: TxContext' found., instead of a null in production logs.
steps.code: // 3. open the context where the transaction id is known fun onMessage(record: PaymentCommand) { context(TxContext(record.txId)) { capture(record.paymentId) } } // capture("pay_7") // error: no context argument for 'tx: TxContext' found.

alt.html: void onMessage(PaymentCommand record) { capture(new TxContext(record.txId()), record.paymentId()); }

steps.say: Check the price: each function in the chain gets one more JVM parameter, and nothing else. No ThreadLocal, no lookup, and the value follows the call, not the thread, so it survives a hop to another thread or a coroutine. Keep MDC for the logging library if it needs it, and fill it from the context at the edge.

drill.title: Write ensureNotNull with a contract, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write ensureNotNull(value, code, lazyMessage) that returns the value as non-null, throws PaymentRejected when it's null, and gives callers a smart cast on the variable they passed. Include the opt-in. Then write the Java version. What does the Kotlin compiler check about your contract?

answer.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T : Any> ensureNotNull(value: T?, code: String, lazyMessage: () -> String): T { contract { returns() implies (value != null) // callers get a smart cast callsInPlace(lazyMessage, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) } if (value == null) throw PaymentRejected(code, lazyMessage()) return value } // it checks that contract { } comes first and warns on some callsInPlace mistakes; // it never checks that the body keeps the returns-implies promise

alt.title: Ensure.java
alt.html: static <T> T ensureNotNull(T value, String code, Supplier<String> message) { if (value == null) throw new PaymentRejected(code, message.get()); return value; // Java has no smart casts, so callers use the return value }

recap: The compiler never reads the body of a function you call, so your own check functions give no smart casts until they declare a contract.
returns() implies cond gives callers a smart cast after a normal return. callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE) lets them initialize a val inside the lambda.
Contracts are Experimental in Kotlin 2.4 and need @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class). The compiler trusts them without checking; a lie becomes a ClassCastException at run time.
Context parameters, context(tx: TxContext) fun ..., are Stable since Kotlin 2.4.0. The compiler fills them by type from enclosing context parameters, context(...) { } blocks and implicit receivers.
On the JVM they are leading parameters (context, then receiver, then the rest), so Java passes them by hand and adding one breaks binary compatibility.
Avoid the parts that aren't stable yet: explicit context arguments and callable references to such functions.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why ensure(req.currency != null, "CURRENCY_MISSING") { ... } followed by req.currency.uppercase() compiles only with a contract, and what the compiler does and doesn't check about that contract.
explain.answer: The compiler decides smart casts inside one function at a time. It doesn't read the body of ensure when it compiles the caller, so without help it has no idea that ensure only returns when the condition is true, and req.currency stays a String?. The contract returns() implies condition, written as the first statement of ensure, is a promise stored in the Kotlin metadata: if this function returns normally, the condition holds. When the caller is compiled, the compiler reads that promise and treats currency as non-null after the call. It doesn't verify the promise. If the body of ensure returned without checking, the code would still compile and fail later at run time. The compiler checks only the form: the opt-in is there, the block is the first statement, and for callsInPlace it warns about some obvious misuse such as calling the lambda twice or storing it. So the body should be as simple as the promise, here a single if (!condition) throw.

deeper.html:
Kotlin 2.4.0 added one more Experimental contract effect, returnsResultOf(), to help the new unused-return-value checker. It needs the flag -Xallow-returns-result-of, and the release notes warn that using it "produces pre-release binaries that earlier Kotlin compiler versions can't read". Keep it out of libraries that others consume.

The extended contracts from Kotlin 2.2.20 behave in an interesting way on the 2.4.21 compiler. Their old -X flags (-Xallow-contracts-on-more-functions and friends) now print the argument '...' is redundant for the current language version 2.4., and a generic returns(true) implies (this is Ok<T>) or a holdsIn contract compiles without any flag. So they appear to be enabled by default from language version 2.3. They still need their opt-ins, though: returnsNotNull() without @OptIn(ExperimentalExtendedContracts::class) is an opt-in error.

If you're migrating from context receivers, three differences bite. Context parameters must be named (or _), and a context parameter is not a receiver in the body, so log("x") becomes logger.log("x"). this@Logger is gone; use the name or contextOf<Logger>(). And classes can't declare a context any more, only functions and properties.

Finally, a design note. The docs mention "simplified dependency injection" as a use. Treat that carefully in a CDI application. A context parameter is resolved at compile time, at each call site, from what is lexically in scope. CDI resolves beans at startup, from the whole application. They answer different questions: context parameters suit per-call values, and CDI suits long-lived services.
